To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transport of opioids is mediated by transporters and that these transporters may be manipulated to reduce or enhance the effects of opioids.

the blood organ transport of fentanyl and lopremide was reduced by substrates of P-Glycoproten and organic anion protein transporters, respectively, and the CNS effects of the opioids were altered by the substrates.

the brain:plasma partitioning of fentanyl and lopremamide is altered in a competitive substrate-specific manner and that these changes in transport are associated with changes in the electroencephalographic effect of fentanyl and loepremide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of new drug delivery systems (DSD) for the treatment of pain.
the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of fentanyl and lopramide in the presence and in the absence of transport inhibitors in the rat.
the development of novel, nonopioid analgesics that are effective and safe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transport protein inhibition is useful for normalizing individual responses to opioids.
the transport protein inhibition of P-gp and organic anion protein transporters (Oatp) can alter the blood organ transport of fentanyl and lopremide and their CNS effects.

the results from this study support the hypothesis that transport proteins are involved in the transport of fentanyl and lopramide across the BBB, but that they may not be the only mechanism involved in the transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain:plasma ratios for opioids are increased by P-gp inhibition and decreased by Oatp inhibition.
transport proteins are a potential target to modulate the effect of opioids.
the pharmacodynamics of opioids can be modified by transport protein inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transport proteins are organ and drug specific and can be manipulated in order to normalize the response to opioids.
P-gp and other transport proteins can affect the distribution of opioids and that transport proteins can be manipulated in a drug-specific way to affect drug distribution.
P-glycoproteins are not the only proteins that transport drugs in the body.
